t.1.101.2: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: There was a certain brahmin, renowned as Māṇḍavya, steadfast, knowing all the laws of dharma, and firmly established in truth and austerity.
t.1.101.1: What deed was done by Dharma, by which he incurred a curse? And by whose curse, O brahmarṣi, was he born from the womb of a śūdra woman?
t.1.101.3: At the gate of his hermitage, at the foot of a tree, that great ascetic, the great yogin, stood with his arms raised aloft, keeping a vow of silence.
t.1.101.4: When he had remained in that austerity for a long time, robbers carrying stolen goods came to his hermitage, O bull of the Bharatas, pursued by many guards.
t.1.101.5: They deposited the stolen goods in his dwelling, O best of the Kurus, and having deposited them, they hid right there out of fear when the force came in pursuit.
t.1.101.6: When they had hidden themselves, that troop of guards then quickly arrived, and those pursuing the thieves saw the seer.
t.1.101.8: But though the guards spoke to him thus, O king, that ascetic, rich in austerities, uttered no word at all, whether good or bad.
t.1.101.7: Then, O king, they questioned that ascetic, who remained as he was: “By which path did the robbers go, O best of the twice-born? Let us follow that same path, O brahmin, with all speed.”
t.1.101.9: Then those king's men, searching that hermitage, saw there those thieves lying hidden, and the stolen wealth as well.
t.1.101.10: Then suspicion arose in the guards toward that sage; having bound him, they then handed him over to the king, along with the robbers.
t.1.101.11: The king commanded that he be put to death together with those thieves, saying, "Let him be slain!" Unrecognized by the executioners, the great ascetic was impaled upon a stake.
t.1.101.12: Then the guards, having impaled that sage upon a stake, took up those riches and returned to the king.
t.1.101.14: As that great-souled one practiced austerities on the point of the stake, the sages then fell into the deepest distress, O scorcher of foes.
t.1.101.13: But that righteous-souled brahmin seer, impaled upon the stake, did not meet his death even though he went without food for a long time thereafter. He held on to his life-breaths and summoned the seers to him.
t.1.101.15: Having become birds, they gathered at night from all sides and, revealing themselves as far as they were able, asked that best of the twice-born: “We wish to hear, brahman, what sin you have committed.”
t.1.101.17: And the king, having heard about that seer, went out together with his ministers and then sought to appease the most excellent of seers, who was fixed upon the stake.
t.1.101.16: Then that tiger among sages said to those ascetics rich in austerity: “Whom shall I go to with blame? For no one else wrongs me.”
t.1.101.18: Whatever wrong I have done to you out of delusion and ignorance, O best of seers, for that I seek your forgiveness; you should not be angry with me.
t.1.101.19: Thus addressed by the king, the sage then granted him his grace. Having received that grace, the king then had him taken down.
t.1.101.21: The sage wandered about just so, with the stake still lodged inside him, and by that austerity he won worlds hard for others to attain. And from then on he is called Aṇīmāṇḍavya throughout the worlds.
t.1.101.22: That brahmin, knower of the highest truth, went to the abode of Dharma; then, seeing Dharma seated there, the mighty one reproached him.
t.1.101.20: Having taken him down from the point of the stake, he pulled at that stake, and, unable to draw the stake out, he cut it off at the base.
t.1.101.24: You thrust a blade of grass into the tails of little insects; this is the fruit of that deed which has come to you, O ascetic rich in austerities.
t.1.101.23: What evil deed did I unknowingly commit, that I have met with such a result of it? Tell me the truth at once, and behold the power of my austerity!
t.1.101.25: For a slight offense you have inflicted a heavy punishment on me; therefore, Dharma, you shall be born as a man in the womb of a śūdra woman.
t.1.101.27: But because of this offense, and through the curse of that great-souled one, Dharma was born in the form of Vidura from a Śūdra womb.
t.1.101.26: Today I establish in the world a boundary from which the fruit of dharma arises: up to the fourteenth year there shall be no sin, but for those who act thus beyond it, it shall indeed be a fault.
t.1.101.28: Skilled in dharma and in worldly affairs, free from greed and anger, far-sighted, devoted to tranquility, and delighting in the welfare of the Kurus.
